Title
Reinforcement Learning Based Anomaly Detection in Context-Aware Heart Rate
Monitoring Systems
Abstract
Physiological anomaly detection is an important application in the early diagnosis of health
risks and unusual bodily conditions. Conventional machine learning methods tend to use
centralized processing and static models, which might not be adaptable to individual-
specific physiological variations and could pose privacy and latency issues. This paper
proposes an adaptive on-device DQN framework for physiological anomaly detection, with
a focus on a new reward adjustment mechanism that can adaptively adjust to varying
physiological patterns. Instead of making a new algorithmic contribution, the novelty of the
proposed method is in combining on-device learning constraints with an adaptive reward
mechanism that can enhance anomaly detection sensitivity and personalization. The
proposed method is tested with physiological signal data under simulated device
conditions and shows its feasibility and efficacy. The experimental results show that
adaptive reward adjustment can improve detection performance over static reward
mechanisms. Physical deployment on wearable hardware is identified as future work.
Keywords: DQN, Physiological Signals, Anomaly Detection, On-device Learning, Adaptive
Reward Mechanism
1. Introduction
The availability of physiological data through wearable and personal monitoring systems
has made it possible to continuously monitor health and detect anomalies early. Heart
rate and other physiological signals are useful for gaining insights into the physiological
state of an individual. However, it is difficult to detect anomalies in these signals because
of the high variability among individuals, noise, and non-stationarity. Most of the existing
methods use supervised or unsupervised learning models that are trained in centralized

settings. Although these methods are efficient, they are not adaptable to individual-level
changes and pose privacy issues when personal health data is sent to cloud servers.
Furthermore, traditional models are not capable of handling dynamic physiological
changes due to stress, activity, or health changes. Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a
promising technique that allows systems to learn from interactions and feedback received
from the environment. RL is particularly suitable for dealing with temporal dependencies
as well as adapting decision-making policies over time. In recent years, on-device learning
has emerged as a promising solution for dealing with challenges associated with latency,
data privacy, and adaptation. This paper describes an adaptive on-device reinforcement
learning framework for physiological anomaly detection using Deep Q-Learning (DQN). The
main contribution of this paper does not lie in the development of a new algorithm but in
the effective combination of on-device reinforcement learning with a reward function
dynamically adjusted according to the characteristics of physiological signals. The
proposed adaptive approach allows the system to adapt to changing signal patterns while
being subject to practical device-level computational limitations.
2. Related Work
Reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied in several healthcare-oriented studies to
enable adaptive and personalized decision-making. Yom-Tov et al. employed Q-learning to
encourage physical activity among diabetes patients through personalized goal settings,
demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive feedback in influencing user behavior. Other
research has utilized Q-learning in Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs) to improve
energy efficiency by optimizing sensor data transmission, focusing primarily on system-
level performance rather than health data interpretation. Reinforcement learning has also
been explored for time-series anomaly detection, where RL-based and active learning
methods adaptively identify anomalous patterns in sequential data. Additionally, recent
studies have proposed reinforcement learning based dynamic health monitoring
frameworks that adjust monitoring strategies based on user activity; however, such
approaches often rely on complex models and non-physiological inputs, such as video
data, which limit their applicability in resource-constrained environments. Overall, existing
works either emphasize behavioral intervention, communication efficiency, or
computationally intensive architectures, leaving a gap in lightweight, on-device
reinforcement learning approaches specifically designed for physiological anomaly
detection.

3. System Overview
The proposed framework is intended for on-device implementation and functions under
limited computational and memory capabilities. The system analyzes physiological signals
on the device and uses a DQN-based reinforcement learning agent to detect anomalies.
3.1 Architecture
The system consists of the following components:
Physiological signal input module
Feature extraction and normalization
DQN agent
Adaptive reward-adjustment mechanism
Rule-based validation layer
Anomaly decision module
All processing is performed locally without reliance on cloud-based inference.
3.2 Rule-Based Validation Layer
In addition to the DQN-based learning agent, a lightweight rule-based validation layer is
incorporated to improve decision stability and reduce false alarms. This layer applies
simple physiological constraints, such as plausible heart rate ranges and short-term
consistency checks, to refine the agent s output. The rule-based layer does not replace the
reinforcement learning component; instead, it acts as a post-decision filter that enhances
robustness and interpretability, which is particularly important in health monitoring
applications.
4. Reinforcement Learning Formulation
The anomaly detection task is modeled as a reinforcement learning problem defined by the
tuple (S, A, R, π).
4:
State (S):
The state represents a feature vector derived from physiological signals, including
statistical and temporal characteristics.
Action (A):
The agent selects actions corresponding to anomaly or normal classifications, or
confidence-adjusted decisions.
Reward (R):
The reward reflects detection of correctness and adaptation to physiological variations.
5. Adaptive Reward-Adjustment Mechanism (Core
Contribution)
Unlike static reward functions, the proposed framework employs an adaptive reward-
adjustment mechanism. The reward is dynamically modified based on:
Signal stability
Recent detection confidence
Frequency of anomalies
This mechanism allows the agent to:
Reduce false positives during stable physiological periods
Increase sensitivity during abrupt signal changes
Adapt to individual-specific baseline shifts
The novelty of the work lies in this adaptive integration rather than in a standalone
algorithmic innovation.

6. On-Device Learning Considerations
To emulate on-device deployment, the system is evaluated under constrained conditions:
Limited model size
Restricted memory usage
Local inference and updates
Training and evaluation are conducted using a simulated embedded environment,
validating feasibility without requiring physical hardware deployment. This approach is
consistent with early-stage system validation in academic research.
7. Experimental Evaluation
7.1 Dataset
Publicly available physiological datasets are used for evaluation.
7.2 Results
Results demonstrate improved anomaly detection of accuracy and stability when using the
adaptive reward mechanism and a Rule Based Layer. Learning curves indicate faster
convergence and reduce false alarms compared to static reward approaches.
8. Discussion
The experimental results highlight the effectiveness of integrating adaptive reward
mechanisms with on-device reinforcement learning. While the absence of proper physical
hardware deployment is acknowledged, the simulated evaluation sufficiently
demonstrates feasibility and conceptual validity.
The framework emphasizes personalization and adaptability, which are critical for
physiological monitoring systems. The results support the claim that novelty arises from
integration and adaptive design rather than isolated components.
6:
9. Limitations and Future Work
The current study does not include physical deployment on wearable hardware. Future
work will focus on:
Real-time deployment on embedded devices
Long-term user-specific adaptation studies
10. Conclusion
This paper presented an adaptive on-device reinforcement learning framework for
physiological anomaly detection. By integrating an adaptive reward-adjustment
mechanism with on-device learning constraints and a rule-based layer, the proposed
approach addresses key challenges in personalization, privacy, and adaptability.
Experimental evaluation demonstrates the potential of the framework, establishing a
foundation for future hardware-based deployment, and extended clinical validation.
